directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, sheltered from strong wind which can shred the large leaves. This is among the largest canna cultivars grown, valued almost entirely for its dramatic architectural foliage rather than its flowers, which are small, sparse orange-red, and often withheld except in long, hot growing seasons. Enormous paddle-shaped leaves resembling banana foliage emerge dark green with a narrow maroon-bronze margin and red-flushed veining and stems. In a single season it can reach 8–12 feet, making it a striking focal point or seasonal screen at the back of a tropical-style border.

common_name: Richard Wallace Canna (Classic Heirloom Clear-Yellow Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every two to three years.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun. Introduced in 1902 and still in commerce, this Crozy-group heirloom canna is prized for producing the clearest, truest yellow of any widely grown canna, with lightly ruffled petals and fine orange-red speckling in the throat. Foliage is a fresh apple-green, providing a bright, uncluttered backdrop that lets the flowers stand out. It flowers continuously from midsummer into early autumn atop sturdy stalks; divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: City of Portland Canna (Classic Salmon-Pink Heirloom Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; divide every few years to prevent overcrowding.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun. A garden favorite for more than a century, this heirloom canna produces abundant upright panicles of rich salmon-pink flowers with a yellow throat and fine yellow petal edging, held well above lush mid-green paddle-shaped foliage. It is a reliable, vigorous bloomer from midsummer through fall and tolerates heat and humidity better than many newer hybrids, making it a dependable choice for large containers or tropical-style borders. Established clumps benefit from division every few years to prevent overcrowding and maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Radiance Caladium (Sun-Tolerant Rose-Pink Speckled Strap-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F, 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to a few hours of direct morning sun.

directions: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F, 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade. A University of Florida strap-leaf release bred for outstanding heat and sun tolerance, Radiance carries bright rose-pink leaf centers flecked with light speckling and edged in a clean green margin. Its narrower, more upright strap-shaped leaves and compact mounding habit make it well suited to mixed containers and border edging where broader fancy-leaf types would sprawl. Unlike traditional shade-only caladiums, it holds color and resists leaf scorch in several hours of direct sun given adequate soil moisture.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to a few hours of direct sun; feed lightly on a monthly schedule through summer.

directions: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. A large, sun-tolerant fancy-leaf caladium whose broad, heart-shaped leaves show striking pink-to-cream variegation traced with darker venation, with the exact balance of pale and colored areas shifting noticeably with light exposure. It is one of the more vigorous sun-bred caladium selections, holding leaf size and color well in beds receiving several hours of direct sun, unlike older shade-only fancy-leaf varieties; give it monthly light feeding through summer for the boldest color display.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Plant tubers 2 inches deep once soil has warmed well above 65°F, since cold soil causes rot and stalled growth; keep soil consistently moist through summer.

directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep once soil has warmed well above 65°F, since cold soil causes rot and stalled growth. This lance/strap-leaf caladium produces narrow, elongated pink-centered leaves with ruffled margins and a defined green edge, forming a dense, low mound well suited to edging and mixed containers. Its compact habit and smaller leaf size distinguish it from the broad fancy-leaf types, and it tolerates more sun than most shade-bred caladiums without significant fading. Keep the soil consistently moist and lightly fertilized for continuous new leaf production through summer.

common_name: Dipt in Wine Coleus (Burgundy-Lime Ruffled ColorBlaze Coleus)

planting.note: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade with even moisture; pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushiness.

directions: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade with even moisture. Part of the ColorBlaze series bred for garden performance in sun, this coleus carries small, pointed, serrated leaves in rich burgundy-wine with pink veining and a lime-green rim that can brighten to gold in strong sun. Its upright, well-branched habit fills out quickly and holds color intensity through summer heat better than many older shade-type coleus. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushiness and remove any flower spikes to keep foliage production strong.

planting.note: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade; regular pinching keeps plants dense through the season.

directions: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade. Discovered as a natural sport of the coleus cultivar 'Freckles' and patented in the early 2000s, Sedona carries vigorous, upright-mounding growth with tri-colored leaves blending red-purple, burnt orange, and pale green. It is one of the more heat- and sun-tolerant heirloom-era sun coleus, holding its warm color palette without bleaching out in strong light. Regular pinching keeps plants dense and full-bodied through the season, and removing flower spikes as they form redirects energy into foliage growth.

planting.note: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in partial shade to full sun; more sun intensifies pink and burgundy tones while shade favors more green.

directions: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in partial shade to full sun. This classic vegetatively propagated coleus carries frilly, ruffled leaves with bright magenta-pink centers, veins of deeper burgundy bleeding outward, and a netted lime-green margin, an effect reminiscent of watermelon flesh and rind. More sun intensifies the pink and burgundy tones while shade favors more green, giving gardeners some control over the color balance. Its compact, bushy, mounded habit with smaller leaves makes it well suited to container plantings and border edging.
